stimulus.text: The 1771 map by Thomas Hutchins marks the village of Cahokia on the Mississippi River, near present-day St. Louis. The pre-contact city of Cahokia stood in this same river valley centuries earlier. Archaeologists who have mapped Cahokia describe a city of mounds, plazas, and a wooden palisade. Trade goods from far away reached the city: copper from the Great Lakes and shells from the Gulf Coast.
stimulus.source_note: Map from the shared image pool; Thomas Hutchins (1771), public domain. Archaeological description paraphrased from standard accounts of Cahokia.

source: original; rewritten from original-u1-native-15 against the grounding books (Cahokia-London size comparison); stimulus map by Thomas Hutchins (1771), public domain
stem: Cahokia held something like 10,000 to 20,000 people around 1200, roughly the size of London at the same time. Why do historians emphasize this comparison?

options.text: To prove that London copied its city plan directly from Cahokia.
options.misconception: Claims a borrowing between two cities with no contact at all.

options.text: To show that Cahokia was actually a European colony in disguise.
options.misconception: Turns a Native city centuries old into a European colony.

options.text: To argue that all Native societies built cities the size of London.
options.misconception: Stretches one city's size into a claim about all societies.

options.text: To show a large city grew in North America without Old World contact.

rationales.A: London and Cahokia had no contact, so neither city could have copied the other.
rationales.B: Cahokia was a Native city that reached its height centuries before Europeans arrived in North America.
rationales.C: One city's size proves nothing about all societies, most of which were far smaller.
rationales.D: The comparison highlights independent achievement: a North American city the size of London grew without any contact with Europe.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the size. Cahokia held something like 10,000 to 20,000 people around 1200.
2. Meet its twin. That was roughly the size of London at the same time, a city on the other side of the ocean.
3. Check the date. Cahokia reached this size centuries before any European arrived.
4. Draw the point. A large city grew in North America on its own, without Old World contact, and the twin in London never knew it existed.
Remember: a size comparison is an argument, so ask what the comparison is meant to prove.
